title: Warm climate limited Lyme disease emergence in US counties near the spread front in 2004-2021: odds fell by 68% per 500 C-day above 4,000 after diffusion, forest and state-year controls
abstract: Question: near the spread front of Lyme disease in the eastern United States, does county climate change the probability that a county becomes endemic, and is the limit on the cold side or the warm side? Approach: we used CDC county case counts (2001-2021), Census population, NOAA nClimGrid temperature and USFS forest cover. A county became endemic at the first persistent 3-year incidence of at least 10 per 100,000. A discrete-time logit hazard model compared 12,265 at-risk county-years within 250 km of endemic counties (393 emergences) in the Northeast, Upper Midwest and Mid-Atlantic/South. Controls were diffusion pressure, population, latitude, forest and region-year or state-year fixed effects. Climate was the 1981-2000 degree-day sum above 0 C (DD0, monthly). Results: emergence was flat across cool climates and fell steeply above about 4,500 C-day. Above 4,000 C-day the odds fell by a factor of 0.32 per +500 C-day (95% interval 0.25-0.41; state-cluster bootstrap 0.23-0.67). The result stayed with state-year effects (0.33), in 2004-2012 (0.34) and 2013-2021 (0.28), in the Northeast (0.13) and Mid-Atlantic/South (0.34), with thresholds of 5 and 20 per 100,000, and with data to 2023. Only 8 emergences occurred in 2,055 county-years above 5,000 C-day. Latitude had no effect after climate. Summer (June-August) temperature fitted best. In CDC ArboNET tick surveillance, which does not depend on physician diagnosis, Borrelia burgdorferi presence in ticks also decreased on the warm side (OR 0.36 per 500 C-day). There was no cold limit inside the US: the endemic area reached the Canadian border by about 2008. Limitations: human surveillance bias can remain within states; climate is correlated with host, tick lineage and land-use gradients; the Upper Midwest had too few warm frontier counties; tests of whether 2004-2021 warming moved the warm limit were not identifiable, and a tracking-ratio test failed.

Left: adjusted odds of emergence by 1981-2000 DD0 bin (reference 3,500-4,000 C-day), with diffusion, population, latitude, forest and region-year effects, 95% intervals. Right: raw annual emergence rate for counties within 60 km of an endemic county.

Odds ratio of emergence per +500 C-day above 4,000 C-day across specifications, periods, regions, incidence thresholds and the extension to 2023. Blue: 95% model interval; yellow: 95% state-cluster bootstrap where computed.
